t: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. The probability that it is a king or a heart is:
e: P(king) = 4/52, P(heart) = 13/52 and P(king of hearts) = 1/52, so P(king or heart) = (4 + 13 − 1)/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.

t: A portfolio consists of 60% standard lives with a one-year mortality rate of 0.01 and 40% substandard lives with a rate of 0.04. The probability that a life chosen at random dies within the year is:
e: By the law of total probability: 0.60 × 0.01 + 0.40 × 0.04 = 0.006 + 0.016 = 0.022.

t: In a group, 60% are standard lives (one-year death probability 0.01) and 40% substandard (0.04). Given that a randomly chosen life has died within the year, the probability that it was substandard is approximately:
Two independent lives each have a probability 0.2 of dying within one year. The probability that at least one of them dies within the year is:
e: P(at least one dies) = 1 − P(both survive) = 1 − 0.8 × 0.8 = 1 − 0.64 = 0.36.

t: A life has a probability 0.9 of surviving each year, independently of other years. The probability that the life survives the next 3 years is:
e: The survival probabilities multiply under independence: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729.

t: The mode of the observations 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 9 is:
e: The mode is the value occurring most frequently; 3 appears three times, more than any other value.

t: The variance of the population values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 is:
e: The mean is 3; the squared deviations are 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 with sum 10, so the variance is 10/5 = 2.

t: A group of 100 independent lives each has a probability 0.02 of dying in a year. The mean and variance of the number of deaths are respectively:
e: The number of deaths is Binomial(100, 0.02): mean np = 2 and variance np(1 − p) = 100 × 0.02 × 0.98 = 1.96.

t: For a normally distributed variable, approximately what proportion of values lie within two standard deviations of the mean?
e: The normal distribution has about 68% of values within one standard deviation, 95% within two and 99.7% within three.

e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). E[X] = 0 × 0.7 + 1,00,000 × 0.3 = ₹30,000. The expected value is the probability-weighted average of the possible outcomes.

t: A nominal rate of 8% per annum convertible half-yearly is equivalent to an effective annual rate of:
e: The half-yearly rate is 4%, so the effective annual rate is (1.04)² − 1 = 1.0816 − 1 = 8.16%.

t: Using the 'rule of 72', an investment earning 7.2% per annum compound will approximately double in:
e: Doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ (rate in %) = 72/7.2 = 10 years. Exactly, (1.072)^10 ≈ 2.004.

t: At 10% per annum effective, the present value of ₹12,100 due in 2 years is:
If the effective annual rate of interest is 6% (ln 1.06 = 0.0583), the equivalent constant force of interest is:
e: δ = ln(1 + i) = ln(1.06) = 0.0583 per annum. The force of interest is slightly below the effective rate.

t: If the effective rate of discount is d = 0.06 per annum, the one-year discount factor v is:
e: v = 1 − d = 1 − 0.06 = 0.94. Equivalently, d = 1 − v.

t: An investor pays ₹1,000 today and receives ₹1,100 exactly one year later. The effective annual yield on the transaction is:
e: Solving the equation of value 1,000(1 + i) = 1,100 gives i = 100/1,000 = 10%.

t: At 5% per annum, a₅ = 4.3295 and v⁵ = 0.7835. The value of the annuity-due ä₅ is:

e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). ä₃ = (1 + i) a₃ = 1.10 × 2.4869 = 2.7356, because each payment of the annuity-due falls one year earlier.

t: At 5% per annum, a₅ = 4.3295 and (1.05)⁵ = 1.2763. The accumulated value s₅ of ₹1 per annum paid in arrear for 5 years is approximately:
An annuity of ₹1,000 per annum is payable for 3 years, the first payment being at the end of year 3. At 10% (v² = 0.8264, a₃ = 2.4869) its present value is approximately:
e: This is a 2-year deferred annuity: ₂|a₃ = v² a₃ = 0.8264 × 2.4869 = 2.0552, so the PV ≈ ₹2,055.

t: The central rate of mortality mₓ is defined as:
e: mₓ = dₓ/Lₓ divides the deaths in the year of age by the average number of lives exposed during the year (Lₓ), whereas qₓ = dₓ/lₓ uses the lives at the start of the year.

t: Assuming deaths are uniformly distributed over the year of age, with lₓ = 10,000 and dₓ = 200, the value of Lₓ (number of years lived between ages x and x + 1) is:
e: Under the uniform distribution of deaths Lₓ = lₓ − ½dₓ = 10,000 − 100 = 9,900.

e: ₘ|aₓ = Nₓ₊ₘ₊₁/Dₓ, so ₁₀|a₄₀ = N₅₁/D₄₀ = 14,000/2,000 = 7.

t: For the same term and rate of interest, the value of an n-year temporary life annuity aₓ:ₙ compared with the annuity-certain aₙ is:
e: Each life annuity payment is contingent on survival, so it is discounted for mortality as well as interest and the EPV is smaller than the corresponding annuity-certain.

t: Section 64VB of the Insurance Act 1938 requires that:
o: Premium is received in advance before the risk is assumed
Every policy carries a free-look clause
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). No risk may be assumed unless the premium has been received in advance or is guaranteed in the manner prescribed.

t: If aₓ = 12, the approximate value of the annuity payable monthly in arrear aₓ⁽¹²⁾ (using aₓ⁽ᵐ⁾ ≈ aₓ + (m − 1)/2m) is:
e: aₓ⁽¹²⁾ ≈ aₓ + 11/24 = 12 + 0.4583 = 12.46. Monthly payments in arrear are received on average earlier than a single annual payment at the year-end.

t: For a life aged 30, M₃₀ = 800, M₅₀ = 500 and D₃₀ = 5,000. The net single premium per ₹1 for a 20-year term assurance is:
e: A¹₃₀:₂₀ = (M₃₀ − M₅₀)/D₃₀ = 300/5,000 = 0.06.

t: For a life aged 30, M₃₀ = 800, M₅₀ = 500, D₅₀ = 2,000 and D₃₀ = 5,000. The net single premium per ₹1 for a 20-year endowment assurance is:
Given M₅₀ = 500 and D₃₀ = 5,000, the net single premium per ₹1 for a whole life assurance on a life aged 30 deferred 20 years is:
e: ₙ|Aₓ = Mₓ₊ₙ/Dₓ = M₅₀/D₃₀ = 500/5,000 = 0.10; it covers death only after age 50.

t: Aₓ (benefit at the end of the year of death) is 0.30 and (1 + i)^½ = 1.03. Under the uniform distribution of deaths, the assurance payable immediately on death Āₓ is approximately:
e: Āₓ ≈ (1 + i)^½ Aₓ = 1.03 × 0.30 = 0.309, because the benefit is paid on average half a year earlier.

t: Under a pure endowment contract, if the life assured dies before the end of the term:
o: the sum assured is paid immediately
the sum assured is paid at the end of the term
e: A pure endowment pays only on survival to the end of the term; death within the term extinguishes the benefit (unless a return-of-premium rider is added).

t: Nomination and assignment of a life insurance policy are governed respectively by which sections of the Insurance Act 1938?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 39 deals with nomination; Section 38 with assignment and transfer.

e: Rₓ is the second summation of Cₓ and gives the value of an assurance whose sum assured increases by 1 each year: (IA)ₓ = Rₓ/Dₓ. Sₓ is the analogous function for increasing annuities.

Which of the following is NOT normally included when converting a net premium into an office (gross) premium?
o: A margin for profit and contingencies
e: The gross premium adds loadings for initial and renewal expenses and for profit/contingencies to the net premium. The reserve is a liability built up from premiums, not a loading within the premium.

t: A whole life assurance of ₹1,000 on a life aged x has premiums payable for 10 years only. If Aₓ = 0.36 and äₓ:₁₀ = 8, the net annual premium is:
e: ₁₀Pₓ = Aₓ/äₓ:₁₀ = 0.36/8 = 0.045 per ₹1 = ₹45 per ₹1,000, higher than the whole-life-premium rate because the same benefit is funded over fewer payments.
